pains.t: Campaign pop-ups and crowded home screens push food delivery users away
pains.w: UXR#273 (Sweden, Norway, Austria, Czech Republic; 2024): EU food delivery users call foodora's time-limited promos and campaign pop-ups FOMO marketing and find Wolt cleaner. UXR#360 (2026): new and existing foodora food delivery users find the home screen busy, with many banners competing for attention. UXR#372 (Turkey, 2026): on Getir, pop-ups at app open and constant notifications alienate food delivery users, and some switch notifications off entirely.

pains.t: Food delivery users have no price loyalty: they compare apps side by side and switch for the better deal
pains.w: UXR#283 (Hong Kong, 2024): food delivery users tie no brand to being cheaper, so they compare apps side by side before ordering. UXR#372 (Turkey, 2026): all 8 interviewed food delivery users on Getir name campaigns and discounts as a trigger to switch apps.

quote.text: At the end of the day, I choose what's the cheapest and what fits my requirements at that moment, the best.

pains.t: PRO value stays invisible: food delivery users neither see their savings nor remember their benefits
pains.w: UXR#381 (Singapore, Malaysia, Philippines, Sweden, Hungary; 2026): PRO subscribers notice no explicit sign that support is prioritised; 4 of 9 want a Home screen icon or pop-up and 3 of 9 want an email. UXR#305 (Singapore, Philippines, Hong Kong, Hungary, Czech Republic, Austria; 2025): low-frequency subscribers lack savings awareness, subscribers click around to find PRO deals, and those familiar with one vertical forget their benefits in the others. High-frequency subscribers are sure the plan pays for itself and do not track savings.

quote.text: Currently I need to click around and find PandaPro.

pains.t: Discounts win a food delivery user's order but not their loyalty
pains.w: UXR#372 (Turkey, 2026): loyalty discounts feel meaningless or irrelevant to food delivery users on Getir: a small TL discount on a large basket, and restaurant deals never used. Desk research (UXR#269, 2024): incentives win preference but do not by themselves build engagement, and for EU food delivery users incentives decide preference without building loyalty.

quote.text: A 25 TL discount on a 900 TL order means nothing.

pains.t: Food delivery users are only moderately confident their data is handled safely: 3.56 of 5 across 4 markets
pains.w: UXR#310 (survey, 2025; Hungary, Austria, Philippines, Malaysia; n=1,280): average confidence in how personal data is handled is 3.56 of 5. Security of personal and financial information and sharing with third parties each worry about 26% of food delivery users. Malaysia is lowest at 3.30 of 5 (n=320).

pains.t: Food delivery users drop PRO when a rival is cheaper or a yearly plan feels like a lock-in
pains.w: UXR#283 (Hong Kong, Singapore, Philippines; 2024): all interviewed Hong Kong food delivery users were uninterested in the foodpanda subscription given Keeta's low prices, and one cancelled pandapro after trying Keeta. Monthly plans let Grab subscribers cancel quickly, while a yearly pandapro subscriber in the Philippines felt locked in and expected to cancel afterwards.

quote.text: I am a hostage to the one-year payment. I might cancel afterwards.

pains.t: Distinctive restaurants and caring service pull EU food delivery users to Wolt
pains.w: UXR#273 (Sweden, Norway, Austria, Czech Republic; 2024): local, trendy and exclusive restaurants sit on Wolt, while foodora's many pizza places taste alike. Some food delivery users switched after poor support experiences on foodora, and stay with Wolt because they never hit a problem.

quote.text: All pizza places in foodora taste the same.

pains.t: The brands are familiar but not distinctive: food delivery users call them generic and overwhelming
pains.w: UXR#360 (unmoderated, 2026; Singapore, Sweden, Norway, Philippines, Turkey, Austria, Czech Republic, Hungary): foodpanda reads as the most familiar, modern and friendly of the three brands, yet is still called generic and overwhelming. foodora is familiar but generic and overwhelming, and Yemeksepeti is modern-leaning but relatively confusing. New foodora food delivery users in Sweden, Norway, Austria, the Czech Republic and Hungary score the current design 2.82 of 5 on generic versus unique.

pains.t: In the Czech Republic, food delivery users treat ordering as a lapse from a healthy, planned life
pains.w: Seen in CCP market visits only (Czech Republic, Q1 2026, CCP#1): food delivery users see the app as something to use when slipping from a healthy, planned lifestyle, so they use it rarely.

delights.t: Fast, clear support makes PRO subscribers feel prioritised, even when nobody tells them
delights.w: UXR#381 (Singapore, Malaysia, Philippines, Sweden, Hungary; 2026): the speed of the Help Center signals PRO value to food delivery users who were never told that support is prioritised.

quote.text: It was so quick I assumed I was already being prioritized.

delights.t: A wider restaurant range wins food delivery users back from cheaper rivals in Hong Kong
delights.w: UXR#283 (Hong Kong, 2024): food delivery users see Keeta as having fewer restaurants and its cheap offers as lower quality, and some returned to foodpanda for restaurants Keeta lacks.

pains.t: QC users do not know the app sells fresh food, pharmacy or specialty shops
pains.w: UXR#312 (Sweden, 2025): QC users do not expect fresh meat, fish and bakery on a delivery app and buy them in store. UXR#296 (2024; six markets): QC users are surprised to find pharmacy, flowers and meat deli when they first open the shop list. UXR#372 (Turkey, 2026): QC users on Getir see one app for food and groceries and see Yemeksepeti as food-only, so they do not order groceries there.

quote.text: I actually didnt know Foodora has these to be honest.

pains.t: Assumed high prices is the top reason new QC users never try QC: 39% across 10 markets
pains.w: UXR#317 (survey, 2025; Singapore, Hong Kong, Philippines, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sweden, Austria, Hungary, Finland, Turkey): 39% of new QC users (n=580) cite assumed unaffordability, and lower prices is the top trigger to try (62% of new QC users who use no other app, n=356). CCP#2 (2026; Hungary, Norway, Philippines, Singapore): delivery and service fees make QC feel pricier than a store, several QC users avoid ordering groceries at all, and the free-delivery minimum is not shown up front.

pains.t: Missing items is the top reason existing QC users go to a competitor or a store: about 53% across 10 markets
pains.w: UXR#317 (survey, 2025; 10 markets): 53.5% cite missing items versus competitors (n=1,516) and 53.4% versus in-store (n=1,096), peaking at 61% in APAC markets. CCP#1 (2026; Hong Kong, Sweden, Czech Republic): QC users go to other apps when they cannot find what they want, citing too little variety, fresh produce and multi-vendor ordering.

pains.t: New QC users do not trust fresh produce online: 4.0 of 7 in 5 markets, against 5.7 in stores
pains.w: UXR#317 (survey, 2025; Hong Kong, Malaysia, Philippines, Pakistan, Singapore; n=2,265): new QC users rate the quality of fresh produce on the app 4.0 of 7, against 4.9 for existing QC users, 5.1 on competitor apps and 5.7 in physical stores. CCP#2 (2026; Hungary, Norway, Philippines, Singapore): QC users cannot verify ripeness or condition of produce, meat and baked goods online, and for some this is why they avoid QC groceries entirely.

pains.t: QC users see QC as an urgent top-up, so larger planned shops go elsewhere
pains.w: UXR#317 (survey, 2025; 10 markets): 26% of QC users who order out of urgency say the service is mainly for urgent purchases (n=1,078), and 37-45% of shoppers go to competitors or stores for larger planned hauls. Desk research (UXR#302, 2024): restock is rare on our platform but common in people's lives, and large supermarket platforms win it on range, price and local availability.

pains.t: Stores win new QC users on inspiration: 32% across 10 markets find offline shopping more inspiring
pains.w: UXR#317 (survey, 2025; 10 markets): 32% of new QC users (n=580) say offline shopping is more inspiring, for discovering new products and shopping with family. UXR#312 (Sweden, 2025): online grocery is a targeted, deals-led trip for bulky or urgent items and exclusive brands, while in-store shopping is routine and inspirational.

pains.t: Not knowing QC exists is a smaller barrier than price or range, but real: 8% of new QC users across 10 markets
pains.w: UXR#317 (survey, 2025; 10 markets): 8% of new QC users (n=580) and 11.8% of existing QC users versus competitors (n=1,516) cite not being aware, rising to 14% in the EU. UXR#283 (Hungary, 2024): food delivery users who order restaurant food rarely noticed the post-order QC cross-sell and often buy groceries offline.

quote.text: I normally just buy (grocery) offline but might try this again.

pains.t: QC users take the home-screen grocery shortcut for the only grocery option
pains.w: UXR#296 (Singapore, Philippines, Hong Kong, Norway, Sweden, Austria; 2024): the highlighted Dmart shortcut is taken as the only option, so some QC users never open the shop list and bounce when Dmart lacks an item. UXR#312 (Sweden, 2025): all 4 interviewed QC users go straight to the foodora Market, by habit and because they do not know other shops are available.

quote.text: I just click here (dmart shortcut), easy.

pains.t: Discount campaigns move QC users between apps in Turkey
pains.w: UXR#372 (Turkey, 2026): all 8 interviewed QC users on Getir name campaigns and discounts as a trigger to switch apps, and attachment to the brand is low.

pains.t: PRO's free-delivery pitch misses QC users who already get free delivery
pains.w: UXR#296 (2024; six markets): in the cart, the PRO free-delivery banner does not appeal to active QC users who already reach free delivery.

quote.text: This Pro free delivery (banner), I never use it cause I always get the free delivery already.

delights.t: Once found, specialty shops delight QC users
delights.w: UXR#296 (2024; six markets): on first opening the shop list, QC users were surprised and pleased to find pharmacy, meat deli and flower shops, and some could see themselves buying from them.

quote.text: Theres more stuff than I expected

jtbd.functional: Restock or top up quickly when an item or time is short, without paying more than in the shop.
jtbd.emotional: Feel sure the produce will be fresh and the price fair before I trust the app with my groceries.
jtbd.social: Do the shop together with my partner or family, as I do in the store.

pains.t: Pickup users find out Pickup exists only at checkout, if at all
pains.w: UXR#341 (Malaysia, Taiwan, Finland; 2025): Pickup users often realise only at checkout that they can collect, the entry is just a small icon, and one participant in Finland did not know it was a button or that Pickup was an option. UXR#312 (Sweden, 2025): QC participants were unaware Pickup exists and could not find its entry point when prompted. Pickup awareness evidence comes from checkout and QC studies, not Pickup-specific research.

quote.text: sometime I only realize here that I I can go and pick up.

pains.t: Collecting on the way is a latent draw for Pickup users: 17% of new QC users across 10 markets would order if they could
pains.w: UXR#317 (survey, 2025; 10 markets): 17% of new QC users (n=154) say they would order if they could pick the order up on the way, and 8% of existing QC users (n=1,800) say it made them order last time. This Pickup signal comes from a QC survey, not Pickup-specific research.
